Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 52 years old, and I'm a male. I'm here because I've been having these headaches for a few months, and it turns out there's a mass on my pituitary gland.
Doctor: When was the pituitary mass discovered, and what was the size of the mass? Have you experienced any vision changes, hormonal imbalances, or fatigue associated with the mass or headaches?
Patient: The mass was discovered a few months ago when I was being checked for the headaches. I didn't know about it until my doctor told me. I haven't had any hormonal issues or fatigue, but I have been bumping into door frames, which I guess is because of my vision. I didn't realize I had a vision problem until the doctor tested me.
Doctor: Could you provide details about the size and location of the pituitary mass, as well as any prior medical evaluations or treatments related to it?
Patient: The doctor mentioned that the mass is pressing on the optic chiasm, and it was discovered during an MRI. I don’t know the exact size, but it’s significant enough to cause vision issues. I haven’t had any other treatments for it yet, just the initial tests.
Doctor: Could you provide the exact size of the pituitary mass as measured on the MRI, and have you undergone any visual field testing or hormonal assessments such as blood tests for pituitary hormones?
Patient: I don’t know the exact size of the mass, but the doctor said it’s significant enough to be pressing on the optic chiasm. I haven’t had any visual field testing yet, but I did have blood tests for pituitary hormones, and my TSH was low, though everything else was normal.
Doctor: Could you please describe the nature and frequency of your headaches, and have you noticed any other neurological symptoms such as double vision, difficulty with balance, or changes in your sense of smell?
Patient: The headaches are located behind my eyes and feel like a dull, nagging ache. They've been getting worse over the past few months, starting at about a 3 out of 10 and now around a 6 out of 10. They tend to be worse in the morning and last a few hours at a time. I haven’t had double vision or balance issues, but I have been bumping into door frames, which I now know is because of my vision loss. I didn’t notice any changes in my sense of smell, though.
Doctor: Has the patient undergone visual field testing yet, and if not, when is it planned? Additionally, could you provide the exact size of the pituitary mass as measured on the MRI?
Patient: I haven’t had the visual field testing yet, but the doctor mentioned it’s going to be scheduled soon, probably before the surgery. As for the size of the mass, I don’t know the exact measurements, but it’s significant enough to be pressing on the optic chiasm.

Doctor: Could you confirm whether the MRI report specifies the size and dimensions of the pituitary mass?
Patient: I don’t know the exact size or dimensions of the mass, but the doctor said it’s significant enough to be pressing on the optic chiasm. The MRI was reviewed, but specific measurements weren’t mentioned to me.

Patient: I haven’t noticed any changes in my vision, like difficulty seeing to the sides, and I haven’t had any changes in my sense of smell. I haven’t had the visual field testing yet, but it’s going to be scheduled before the surgery.

Patient: I don’t know the exact dimensions of the mass, but the doctor said it’s a significant mass pressing on the optic chiasm. Specific measurements weren’t mentioned to me during our conversation.

Patient: I haven’t noticed any changes in my peripheral vision, like difficulty seeing to the sides, and I haven’t had any issues with visual acuity or color vision. The doctor mentioned I have bitemporal hemianopia, but I didn’t realize it until he tested me during the exam.
